pull.title: net_processing: set fDisconnect instead of calling DisconnectNode
pull.body: `MaybeDiscourageAndDisconnect` calls `DisconnectNode` which creates a `CSubNet` containing only the `CNode`'s address. This will disconnect every `CNode` with the same IP address. This is normally not a problem, except for clearnet-over-tor. If a node has an honest clearnet-over-tor inbound connection, the IP of the inbound peer will be the exit node's IP address. If an attacker connects to the node through the same exit node and sends an invalid message, they can cause every inbound peer sharing the exit node's IP to get disconnected. Fix this by only disconnecting the misbehaving `CNode` rather than every `CNode` sharing the IP.

Misbehaviour used to result in an address ban prior to #19219, but now it just optimises who gets disconnected when our connections are full; so I think disconnecting all peers on the same address used to be consistent behaviour but now is not.

d698b75f8bd20a634f66b0307fd18b79ebbda9c0 -> d63068c

removes the `disconnect_private_broadcast` argument from `DisconnectNode`

Did well addressing earlier concerns.

Approach ACK / tACK d63068c

lgtm ACK d63068c58ec9fcc94876bce30865d1a7266d64d4

Tested on my server with two addnode connections from a single IPv4.

If someone wants to test this with a unit test:

```diff
diff --git a/src/test/denialofservice_tests.cpp b/src/test/denialofservice_tests.cpp
index a5e7c90..86c5271 100644
--- a/src/test/denialofservice_tests.cpp
+++ b/src/test/denialofservice_tests.cpp
@@ -402,3 +402,3 @@ BOOST_AUTO_TEST_CASE(peer_discouragement)
                          /*addrNameIn=*/"",
-                         /*conn_type_in=*/ConnectionType::PRIVATE_BROADCAST,
+                         /*conn_type_in=*/ConnectionType::INBOUND,
                          /*inbound_onion=*/false,

Leaving a note in case it interests anybody:

I haven't tested this, I think this change also prevents an attacker from disconnecting a normal A <-> B connection where A is running linux and the attacker knows they are connected:
- attacker sends ~4096 SYN packets to A to fill up the half-open queue
- A falls back to SYN cookies
- attacker sends ACK packets to A that guess the cookie value to try and forge another connection between A <-> B
  - the ACK packets also contain in their data a version, verack, and invalid headers message (all in a single packet)
- A will accept the connection if the cookie value is correct (a 8 in 2^32 guess, the probability of guessing a cookie value is greater than guessing the ephemeral port number, a sequence number in the window, and an ack number in the window)
  - if A processes the version, verack, and headers message before B can send a RST (if B does this, it depends), A will disconnect all CNode's matching B's IP including the honest, pre-existing A <-> B connection
